questions.question: What is the 2026 multi-agent AI SRE architecture pattern?
options: A single AI agent with full autonomous remediation authority over all infrastructure
A supervisor agent coordinating specialized agents (logs, metrics, runbooks) with humans approving judgment calls
Three independent AI agents running in parallel with the fastest one's answer winning
An AI copilot that only answers questions but never proposes actions
questions.explanation: The 2026 pattern is a supervisor coordinating specialized agents — one for logs, one for metrics, one for runbooks — where AI proposes hypotheses and queries, but humans approve judgment calls. Datadog Bits AI and Azure SRE Agent ship this architecture.

questions.question: What MIT research result does the lesson cite about pre-incident prediction?
options: An LLM predicted 65% of outages 5 minutes early
An LLM trained on historical logs, GPU temps, and API error patterns predicted 89% of outages 10-15 minutes early
A transformer model predicted 99% of outages 1 minute early
No LLM has yet achieved better than 50% outage prediction
questions.explanation: MIT research reports an LLM trained on historical logs plus GPU temperatures plus API error patterns predicted 89% of outages 10-15 minutes in advance. The lesson notes that predictions without actuation are just dashboards — the operational constraint is actuation.

questions.question: What is the NeuBird Hawkeye adversarial evaluation pattern?
options: Two AI models debate the root cause and the longer argument wins
Two models analyze the same incident independently: agreement = confidence, disagreement = escalate to human
One model proposes a fix and another model attacks it for weaknesses
Two models use different datasets; the one with better recall is trusted
questions.explanation: NeuBird Hawkeye's adversarial evaluation runs two models on the same incident independently. When they agree on the diagnosis, confidence is high. When they disagree, the system escalates to a human for judgment. This operationalizes uncertainty quantification.

questions.question: What is the safe scope for fully autonomous AI remediation in 2026?
options: Any action that can be reversed within 24 hours
Narrow, well-defined actions: restart pod, revert a specific deploy, scale within pre-set bounds
All infrastructure changes within a single availability zone
Any action approved by an on-call engineer in real time
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit: fully autonomous action stays narrow — restart pod, rollback a specific deploy, scale within bounds. Anything broader requires human approval. The lesson calls out that 'set it and forget it' sales pitches are overselling.

questions.question: What is the lesson's projection for automated LLM failover adoption by end-2026?
options: 25% of enterprise LLMs
50% of enterprise LLMs
75% of enterprise LLMs
95% of enterprise LLMs
questions.explanation: The lesson cites a projection that 95% of enterprise LLMs will have automated failover by end-2026 — reflecting rapid adoption of AI SRE patterns and the operational maturity of the ecosystem.

questions.question: Why do AI SRE systems use RAG to ground LLMs in infrastructure data rather than prompting the model with its training knowledge?
options: RAG is faster than prompting at inference time
Infrastructure data (live logs, runbooks, topology) is not in the model's training data and changes constantly
RAG avoids the need for fine-tuning on expensive GPU hardware
Regulatory requirements mandate that all AI decisions reference live data
questions.explanation: Live infrastructure state — current logs, service topology, today's runbook versions — cannot be in training data. RAG injects the relevant live context into the model's prompt, grounding hypothesis generation in current reality rather than stale training knowledge.
